rewritten_text:
She left everything behind, saving only the memory that these things had existed.

Since departing from Lady Russell's house in September, Anne had never been inside Kellynch. There had been no necessity; and on the few occasions when a visit to the Hall might have been possible, she had managed to avoid it. Her first return was to take up her accustomed place in the Lodge's elegant modern rooms, and to bring pleasure to the eyes of its mistress.

Lady Russell's delight at seeing her was mingled with a little apprehension. She knew who had lately been a visitor at Uppercross. Happily, however, Anne had either grown fuller and improved in appearance, or Lady Russell imagined that she had; and as Anne received the resulting compliments, she amused herself by linking them to her cousin's unspoken admiration, and by hoping that a second spring of youth and beauty might be granted her.

Once their conversation began, she quickly perceived some alteration in her own mind. The matters that had filled her heart upon leaving Kellynch, which she had thought neglected and had been obliged to suppress among the Musgroves, now held only a lesser interest. Of late she had almost forgotten even her father, her sister, and Bath. Their affairs had been submerged beneath those of Uppercross. When Lady Russell returned to their old expectations and anxieties, expressing pleasure in the house they had taken in Camden Place and regret at Mrs Clay's continued presence, Anne would have been ashamed to confess how much more her thoughts dwelt upon Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and all her friends there. The home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick interested her far more than her own father's residence in Camden Place, or her sister's intimacy with Mrs Clay. She was positively obliged to make an effort to appear to share Lady Russell's concern for subjects which naturally had the strongest claim upon her attention.

Their conversation upon another matter began with some constraint. The accident at Lyme could not go unmentioned. Lady Russell had scarcely been five minutes in the place on the previous day before the entire account was poured out to her; nevertheless, it must be discussed again. She must ask questions, deplore the rashness, and lament its consequence; and both must utter Captain Wentworth's name. Anne knew that she managed it less easily than Lady Russell. She could not pronounce the name while meeting Lady Russell's eyes directly until she had resorted to giving a brief account of what she believed concerning the attachment between him and Louisa.

The studio was full of the rich fragrance of roses. Whenever the light summer breeze stirred the garden trees, the strong scent of lilac or the gentler perfume of the pink-flowered thorn drifted in through the open door.

Lord Henry Wotton lay in the corner of a couch made of Persian saddlebags, smoking cigarette after cigarette, as he usually did. From there he could just see the glowing blossoms of a laburnum, sweet and golden as honey. Its trembling branches seemed barely strong enough to support their own fiery beauty. Now and then the strange shapes of flying birds passed as shadows over the long raw-silk curtains drawn across the great window. For an instant they looked like Japanese pictures, reminding him of those pale, jade-faced painters of Tokyo who tried to capture speed and movement in an art that must itself remain still. Bees hummed dully as they pushed through the long, uncut grass or circled persistently around the dusty golden trumpets of the spreading honeysuckle. Their sound seemed to make the silence more oppressive. The faint rumble of London resembled the low, sustained note of an organ far away.

In the middle of the room, fastened to an upright easel, was a full-length portrait of an exceptionally beautiful young man. A short distance in front of it sat the painter, Basil Hallward. His sudden disappearance some years ago had caused great public excitement at the time and inspired many strange theories.

As the artist studied the graceful, handsome figure he had captured so skilfully, a pleased smile crossed his face and seemed ready to remain there. But suddenly he sprang up, shut his eyes, and pressed his fingers against his eyelids, as if trying to hold some strange dream inside his mind for fear he might wake from it.

“It is your finest work, Basil, the best thing you have ever painted,” Lord Henry said lazily. “You really must send it to the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is too big and too vulgar. Every time I have been there, either there have been so many people that I could not see the pictures, which was dreadful, or so many pictures that I could not see the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor is the only possible place.”

“I don't believe I'll send it anywhere,” the painter replied, throwing his head back in the peculiar way that had made his friends laugh at him when he was at Oxford.

“One more word, Rose. Dearest Rose, just one!” Harry cried, throwing himself in front of her. “If I had been less—less fortunate, as the world would put it—if I had been destined for a quiet, unknown life, if I had been poor, ill, helpless, would you have rejected me then? Or is it the prospect of my gaining wealth and distinction that has raised this objection?”

“Please don't make me answer,” Rose replied. “Those circumstances do not exist, and never will. It is unfair, almost unkind, to insist on asking.”

“If your answer is what I almost dare to hope,” Harry replied, “it would bring a little happiness to my lonely life and brighten the road ahead. A few short words could do so much for someone who loves you more than anything; that is no small thing. Oh, Rose, for the sake of my deep and lasting love, for everything I have suffered for you and everything you are condemning me to suffer, answer this one question!”

“Then, if your life had been different,” Rose answered, “if you had been a little above me in society, instead of so far above; if I could have helped and comforted you in some modest, peaceful home, away from the world, instead of being a shame and a hindrance among ambitious, important people, I would not have faced this painful choice. I have every reason to be happy now, very happy; but I admit, Harry, that then I would have been happier.”

As Rose confessed this, memories of hopes she had treasured long ago as a girl crowded into her mind. They brought tears, as old hopes do when they return faded and dead; and crying eased her pain.

“I cannot help this weakness, and it only strengthens my decision,” Rose said, holding out her hand. “I really must leave you now.”

“Promise me one thing,” Harry said. “Once more, and only once—within a year, though perhaps much sooner—let me speak to you about this for the last time.”

“Not to urge me to change a decision I know is right,” Rose replied with a sad smile. “That would be useless.”

“No,” said Harry, “only to hear you repeat it, if you choose—repeat it finally! Whatever position or fortune I have, I will lay it at your feet. If you still hold to your present decision, I will do and say nothing to change it.”

“Then let it be that way,” Rose answered. “It is only one more pain, and by then I may be better able to bear it.”

Again she held out her hand.
